engine.title: Stop buying strength that has already run
engine.body: The 4H RSI ceiling for longs was 75. Splitting every closed trade by the RSI recorded at entry showed the engine bleeding above 65 and profitable below it. The ceiling is now 65.
engine.note: Holds in both halves of the sample and at every cut point tested (60, 65, 70), so it is not one lucky threshold. The threshold was still chosen from this sample, so treat the size as an upper bound.

engine.title: A break-even stop would not have helped
engine.body: The median losing trade was +1.44R in profit before it reversed, and 59% touched a full +1R first. That looks like an obvious fix: move the stop to entry once price pays 1R. Re-walking every trade bar by bar, with winners subject to the same rule, says otherwise.
engine.note: The first version of this test only altered losers, which guarantees a positive answer. Correcting it reversed the conclusion. Nothing tested cleared one standard error, so no stop rule was adopted.

engine.title: Trades were being closed at prices that never traded
engine.body: The grader had never resolved a single trade — an exception was being swallowed silently — leaving a fallback path that could book an exit at a bar from before the signal existed. Every closed trade was re-graded against bars that actually printed.
evidence: exits corrected to a real price
engine.note: This moved the headline number against me. It is published anyway, because the earlier number was not real. Pre-correction data is kept in the repo rather than deleted.

engine.title: A first target must pay back the risk
engine.body: T1 was whichever structural level sat nearest the entry, with no distance test. One signal shipped a T1 worth 0.19R against its own stop, printed beside an R:R of 2.41 quoted off T2. T1 must now return at least 1R.

chess.title: Tactics: Discovered Attack
chess.body: Moving one piece reveals an attack from another. The moved piece itself may also attack something. Discovered checks are devastating — the opponent must deal with the check while you capture elsewhere. Pattern: move a blocking piece with tempo, reveal a rook/bishop attack. Double attacks are impossible to fully defend.

wisdom.title: On Discipline and Freedom
wisdom.body: The most disciplined people are the freest. Akshay who wakes at 6am, exercises, studies, then works has more hours and more energy than the one who stays up late and drags through mornings. Discipline is choosing what you want most over what you want now. It's the highest form of self-respect.

book.author: Cal Newport
book.chapter: The Any-Benefit Mindset vs The Craftsman Mindset
book.lesson: Most people adopt the any-benefit mindset for tools: if a tool provides any benefit, use it. This is why everyone is on every social platform, attending every meeting, checking email all day. Newport argues for the craftsman mindset: identify the core factors that determine your success and happiness. Adopt a tool only if its positive impacts on these factors substantially outweigh its negative ones. Your attention is finite. Every tool that fragments it has a cost, even if it has some benefits. The question is never 'is there value here?' but 'is this the best use of my limited attention?'
book.key_quote: Your attention is your most valuable professional asset. Spend it deliberately.
book.action: List your three most important professional skills. Then ask: does checking social media or attending this meeting help or hurt those skills?
crux: Deep work: focused, undistracted, cognitively demanding work. It is becoming rare and simultaneously more valuable.
Two core abilities now decide income: learn hard things fast, and produce elite output fast.
Both abilities depend on deep work. Both are destroyed by fragmented attention.
Shallow work is logistically necessary and infinitely replaceable. It feels like work and produces nothing durable.
Attention residue: switching tasks leaves cognitive drag for 15–20 minutes. Ten switches cost you the day.
High-quality work = time spent × intensity of focus. Intensity is the neglected multiplier.
Four scheduling philosophies: monastic, bimodal, rhythmic, journalistic. Rhythmic — same hours daily — is the only one most people can sustain.
Willpower is finite and depletes. Rituals and fixed locations spend none of it.
Schedule every minute of the workday. Not to obey it, but to force the question 'what deserves this hour?'
Fixed-schedule productivity: hard-stop the day and work backwards. Constraint forces ruthless triage.
Boredom tolerance is trainable and prerequisite. If every queue is filled with a phone, focus never develops.
Quit social media by default; readmit a tool only if it clearly serves a core goal.
Drain the shallows. Aim shallow work under 40% of the week and defend the rest.
learnings: Busy is not a proxy for valuable. It is usually a proxy for unfocused.
The ability to concentrate is a skill you build, not a mood you catch.
Fragmented time is not additive — four 30-minute blocks are worth far less than one 2-hour block.
Downtime is not idleness; unconscious processing needs it.
examples: Carl Jung built a stone tower at Bollingen and wrote there in the mornings, uninterrupted, while running a clinical practice.
Adam Grant compressed teaching into one semester and batched research into the other — becoming one of the most published psychologists of his generation.
Newport wrote a book, earned a PhD, and published peer-reviewed papers while rarely working past 5:30pm, by hard-stopping his day.
adapt: One 90-minute block before 8am for the highest-leverage build. Phone in another room, not face-down on the desk.
Batch Telegram, Instagram, and email into two windows. Notifications off outside them.
Financial models are deep work. Do them before the market opens, never in gaps between messages.
Hard-stop at 7pm on weekdays. The constraint is what forces the triage.

minimalism.title: The Deathbed Filter
minimalism.body: Nobody has ever wished for a larger television. Possessions almost never make the list of what mattered. Use that as a purchasing filter while there is still time to act on it.
minimalism.action: Name three things that would make your list. Spend accordingly.
minimalism.label: Minimalism

etiquette.title: Never Be The Loudest In The Room
etiquette.body: Volume signals insecurity, not authority. The person everyone leans in to hear holds the room. Competence rarely needs amplification.
etiquette.action: In your next meeting, speak one notch quieter than feels natural.
etiquette.label: Etiquette

stillness.title: Eat One Meal In Silence
stillness.body: No phone, no screen, no conversation. Taste the food. Most meals are consumed while attention is elsewhere, which is why they satisfy so little.
stillness.label: Stillness

model.title: Sunk Cost
model.body: Money and time already spent are gone and should not influence the next decision. The only question is the value from here forward.
model.action: Name one commitment you continue solely because of what it has already cost.
model.label: Mental Model

arabic.use: The universal greeting. Reply: wa alaykum as-salaam. Use it entering any room or meeting.
arabic.label: Arabic

drill.title: Keyboard Only
drill.body: Work for ten minutes with no mouse. Excel and modelling speed is mostly navigation, and navigation is mostly shortcuts you have not learned yet.
drill.action: Ten minutes, mouse unplugged. Note every shortcut you had to look up.
drill.label: Drill

health.title: Breathe Through Your Nose
health.body: Nasal breathing improves oxygen uptake, filters air, and produces nitric oxide, which is a vasodilator. Mouth breathing during sleep correlates with poorer sleep quality and dental issues.
health.action: Nasal-only breathing for one Zone 2 session. Pace will drop. That is the point.
health.label: Health

quote.name: Jack Dorsey
quote.quote: Make every detail perfect and limit the number of details to perfect.

lesson.lesson: Do one thing every day that scares you.

case.title: HDFC Bank: The Conservative Compounding Machine
case.story: HDFC Bank has never posted a quarterly loss in 28 years. Never chased exotic products. Just excellent credit underwriting, low NPAs, and consistent execution.
case.lesson: In banking and in life, the boring strategy often wins. Consistency over 20 years beats brilliance in short bursts. Compounding requires not breaking the chain.

fpna.title: CFO Communication
fpna.body: Lead with the number, then variance, then reason, then action. '₹12Cr EBITDA, ₹2Cr below plan, due to X, here's the fix.'

cfo.title: FC Step 5: Treasury Basics
cfo.body: Cash flow forecasting, FX hedging policy, bank relationship management, working capital optimisation. The jump from FP&A to FC often requires you to pick up treasury. Start with 13-week cash flow models.

money_hack.title: NPS for Tax Saving
money_hack.body: ₹50K in NPS under 80CCD(1B) = ₹15K saved at 30% bracket. Plus retirement corpus.

dubai.title: Do not send the same CV twice
dubai.body: One master CV, then a version per pool: retail, logistics, energy, advisory. Same facts, different order, different top five bullets. It takes 20 minutes per version and roughly doubles response rate.
dubai.targets: The bullet at the top of the page is doing 80% of the work.
dubai.action: If the top bullet does not name the sector's core problem, rewrite it.

desk.productivity: Eat the frog: hardest task first, before checking any messages.

father.title: Introduce water in an open cup
father.do: Offer a few sips from a small open cup, held by you. Expect most of it to spill.
father.why: Open-cup drinking develops different oral motor patterns than a bottle or spout. Starting now, badly, is easier than starting later, correctly.

father.title: Massage after the bath
father.do: Two minutes of firm, slow strokes on legs and back after bathing.
father.why: Sustained touch by a father has measurable effects on infant stress response, and it gives you a reliable daily block of contact that is not feeding or settling.

life_wisdom.teaching: Householders take limited versions of the great vows rather than the monastic form — the tradition explicitly designs for people with jobs and families.
life_wisdom.apply: Do not adopt a practice you cannot sustain alongside work and a seven-month-old. A small vow kept beats a large one abandoned.

life_wisdom.teaching: The Buddha told the Kalamas not to accept teaching on authority, tradition, or scripture — but to test whether it leads to benefit when practised.
life_wisdom.apply: Apply it to strategy advice, including from people senior to you. What is the evidence, and what would falsify it? Deference is not evidence.

vocab.meaning: To extend a trend beyond known data.
vocab.example: Do not extrapolate a festive quarter across the year.
vocab.note: Naming the error is often the fastest way to kill a bad forecast.

vocab.meaning: Relating to the next unit; or barely sufficient.
vocab.example: The marginal store adds revenue but no profit.
vocab.note: In economics it means 'the next one'. Most people misuse it to mean 'small'.

speaking.title: One-minute summary
speaking.drill: At the end of the day, summarise it out loud in 60 seconds as if to a CFO.
speaking.why: Daily practice at compressing information is the underlying skill in every senior finance conversation.

interview_tech.q: Gross margin fell 180bps. Walk me through the bridge.
interview_tech.a: Decompose into four drivers: mix — did the sales split shift toward lower-margin categories; price — did you discount more, measured as markdown as a percent of gross sales; cost — did landed cost rise from FX, freight or supplier price; and shrink/wastage. Quantify each in basis points so they sum to 180. The bridge is the answer, not the total. In retail the most common culprit is markdown depth on aged stock, which is really an buying error surfacing one season late.

interview_tech.q: Auditors propose an adjustment you disagree with. What do you do?
interview_tech.a: Separate judgement from fact. If it is a factual error, show the evidence and it goes away. If it is a judgement — provisioning, impairment, lease term — set out your basis in a technical memo: the standard, the specific paragraph, the assumptions and their support. Escalate to the engagement partner if needed, and involve the audit committee chair early rather than late. If they still disagree and it is material, you record it. What you never do is trade an adjustment against a different one.

interview_soft.q: Tell me about a time you were wrong about a person.
interview_soft.a: A quieter question than it looks — it tests self-awareness and whether you revise judgements. Both directions work: someone you underestimated who turned out strong, or someone you backed who did not work out. The second is braver and lands better if you own the hiring or promotion decision. End with what you changed about how you assess people, ideally something structural like a different interview question or a probation checkpoint.

interview_soft.q: If we hire you and in a year it has not worked, what is the most likely reason?
interview_soft.a: A genuinely good question and a rare one. Answer honestly with the real risk, not a disguised strength: a mismatch on decision-making pace, an unclear boundary between your scope and someone else's, or a business where the data foundations are worse than described so the first year goes on plumbing rather than insight. Then say what you would do in month one to check for it. Naming the failure mode makes you look like someone who has thought about the job rather than the offer.
